newsitem.title: USA: Bull spreading seen in CME live cattle from report.
newsitem.headline: Bull spreading seen in CME live cattle from report.

text.p: Bull spreading could dominate CME live cattle futures trade on Monday following Friday's monthly USDA Cattle-On-Feed report, livestock analysts said.
"Bull spreading should prevail in the aftermath of the report," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corporation.

The report showed record-high May marketings at feedlots having at least 1,000 head, while June 1 on-feed supplies also set a record due to May placements that were the second highest on record since the current series of reports started in 1992.
Analysts expect June and August live cattle futures to trade steady to 0.250 cent per lb higher Monday. Deferred months are seen trading steady to 0.250 lower.

USDA reported June 1 on-feed cattle supplies at major 7-state 1,000-head-plus feedlots at 8.226 million head, 113 percent of a year ago and a record since the current series of reports started back in 1992. Placements onto feedlots were the second largest since records started at 1.64 million head, 126 percent of last year. The record of 1.673 million was set in 1995.
The on-feed percentage was near the average analyst estimate of 113.2 percent, while placements were above the high end of estimates that ranged from 110.5 to 124 percent.

But May marketings at 1.818 million head, 104 percent of last year, were also a record, exceeding the 1.747 million head sent to market a year ago. Marketings were two percentage points above the high end of estimates and will have the most impact on nearby live cattle futures.

"The fact that they did a more aggressive marketings job during May than we expected will wrest back from the packers some control in the market, as least temporarily in the next week or two," Levitt said.

The report showed not only that feedlots were aggressive in their marketings, but that non-fed slaughter rates were down. Cow kills were declining and fewer slaughter cattle were coming in from Canada.
"Basically it (the report) suggests that our non-fed, both cows and the other residual non-fed steer and heifer slaughters, dropped sharply," said Tom Tippens, CEO Professional Cattle Consultants.

Tippens also noted that beef production in May was down four percent from last year despite the higher fed marketings. Less beef is being produced from fed cattle compared to last year when part of the kill included more cows and non-fed supplies.

"As we approach what is generally perceived to be our peak supply, you have to tone down the impact of those supplies because all of a sudden they are not necessarily going to translate into bigger production," Tippens said.

The large placement figure will weigh on back months of live cattle futures, especially October and possibly December. Feedlots were just as aggressive in placing cattle as they were in marketing. But the larger percentage increase had been expected by some analysts and this will limit its effect on futures, analysts said.
Tippens said this is "just one of a long line of big placements that we've seen for eight or nine months" compared to low placements onto feed last year.
Analysts agreed that action in cash markets on Monday may have more impact on futures than the report. Expectations of possibly higher fed cattle prices next week had boosted futures on Friday.
